title: Realizing I'd Been Taking Credit Without Meaning To
script: Narrator: [uneasy] It took an uncomfortable comment from a junior colleague to make me realize I'd been unintentionally taking credit for work that wasn't entirely mine.
Narrator: [reflective] During a client presentation, I described a strategy as something I had developed, when in reality it had emerged from a brainstorm with two other people.
Narrator: [honestly] I hadn't meant to erase their contribution deliberately; I'd simply told the story the way it existed in my own memory, which flattered me by default.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Afterward, Wina, who had contributed the original idea, mentioned quietly that she'd noticed her name hadn't come up once during the entire meeting.
Narrator: [defensive] My immediate reaction was to explain myself, insisting it hadn't been intentional, as though intention were the only thing that mattered here.
Narrator: [reflective] But sitting with it overnight, I recognized that impact matters regardless of intention, and the impact on Wina had been real, even if unintended.
Narrator: [honestly] I'd been the one presenting, the one visible in every meeting, so naturally the story kept collapsing into a version where I was the sole author.
Narrator: [determined] The next morning, I emailed the client directly, correcting the record and naming both colleagues as co-authors of the strategy we'd pitched.
Narrator: [nervous] It felt oddly exposing to admit publicly that I'd gotten something wrong, as though correcting it drew even more attention to the original mistake.
Narrator: [surprised] Instead, the client simply thanked me for the clarification, and Wina later told me it meant more to her than I probably realized at the time.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Since then, I've started deliberately naming contributors before presentations even begin, rather than trusting memory to distribute credit fairly on its own.
Narrator: [reflective] It turns out memory is a fairly self-serving narrator, quietly editing out whoever wasn't standing at the front of the room.
Narrator: [warmly] I don't think I'm a fundamentally dishonest person, but I've learned that fairness sometimes requires deliberate correction, not just good intentions left unexamined.
Narrator: [peacefully] Wina and I still work together closely, and if anything, the correction seemed to deepen her trust rather than damage my credibility.

quiz.question: What triggered the narrator's realization?
options: An uncomfortable comment from a junior colleague, Wina, about being uncredited
quiz.explanation: An uncomfortable comment from Wina, noting her name hadn't come up in the meeting, triggered the realization.

options: Described a strategy as her own creation when it had come from a brainstorm with others
quiz.explanation: She described the strategy as something she had developed, when it actually emerged from a brainstorm with two other people.

quiz.question: What was the narrator's first reaction when Wina mentioned it?
options: Defensively explaining that it hadn't been intentional
quiz.explanation: Her immediate reaction was to explain herself defensively, insisting it hadn't been intentional.

options: Emailed the client to correct the record and name both colleagues as co-authors
Apologized privately but said nothing to the client
quiz.explanation: She emailed the client directly, correcting the record and naming both colleagues as co-authors of the strategy.

quiz.question: What has the narrator changed going forward?
options: She deliberately names contributors before presentations rather than trusting memory
She lets others take all the credit
quiz.explanation: She now deliberately names contributors before presentations begin, rather than trusting memory to distribute credit fairly.
